Dance and the agricultural calendar

Traditional Indian dances are frequently associated with particular seasons or festivals. These associations help distinguish dances that may otherwise share similar costumes, instruments or group formations.

The occurrence of a dance during a particular festival does not mean that it can only be performed on that occasion. Many traditional forms are also presented at cultural programmes, fairs and other social gatherings.

Intangible cultural heritage

Intangible cultural heritage consists of living traditions, expressions, knowledge and skills recognised by communities as part of their cultural heritage. Performing arts, oral traditions, rituals, festive events and traditional craftsmanship are important examples.

UNESCO adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2003. Its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity includes numerous Indian cultural practices.

The purpose of recognising intangible cultural heritage is to support awareness, safeguarding and continued transmission of living traditions. Unlike monuments and archaeological sites, these traditions depend fundamentally on the people who practise and transmit them.

Important Indian dance-related inscriptions

Recognised cultural elementYearRegion

Garba and Deepavali: chronological distinction

Garba of Gujarat was inscribed in 2023. Deepavali was subsequently inscribed in 2025 under Decision 20.COM 7.b.24.

Deepavali is recognised as a broader living festival tradition involving religious observances, social gatherings, lamps, music, dance and other community practices. It is not a specific folk dance.

As of 25 November 2026, both Garba of Gujarat and Deepavali remain inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Institutional responsibility in India

The Sangeet Natak Akademi, established in 1952, is India's national academy for music, dance and drama. It functions under the Ministry of Culture and supports the preservation and promotion of performing arts.

It serves as the nodal agency for matters connected with UNESCO's 2003 Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage and maintains India's national inventory of intangible cultural heritage.

The Archaeological Survey of India is primarily concerned with archaeological research and the protection of monuments and archaeological sites. It should not be confused with the Sangeet Natak Akademi's role in coordinating intangible cultural heritage nominations.

Prelims focus

  • UNESCO Convention on Intangible Cultural Heritage: 2003.
  • Chhau, Kalbelia and Mudiyettu: 2010.
  • Manipuri Sankirtana: 2013.
  • Garba of Gujarat: 2023.
  • Deepavali: 2025, after Garba.
  • Trap: Sangeet Natak Akademi, rather than the Archaeological Survey of India, is the nodal agency for the 2003 Convention.

[References: UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003; UNESCO, India: Elements on the Lists, inscription records for 2009-2025; UNESCO Decisions 5.COM 6.15, 5.COM 6.16, 8.COM 8.14, 18.COM 8.b.32 and 20.COM 7.b.24; Ministry of Culture, Annual Report 2023-24, Section 3.3c: Sangeet Natak Akademi; Ministry of Culture, UNESCO Consultant Advertisement dated 19 May 2025; festival associations from the respective state cultural and tourism sources. Inscription status and online references checked 25 November 2026.]

Shared traditions across state boundaries

Chhau has 3 recognised regional styles in Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal. Karma is practised across several states of eastern and central India. Dhemsa or Dhimsa is shared by tribal communities of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. Cham belongs to the wider Himalayan Buddhist cultural tradition.

Regional associations should therefore be understood together with community identity, religious occasion, instruments and distinctive performance objects. These characteristics provide a more precise identification than the state name alone.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat: Garba, Tippani, Padhar, Hudo and Siddi Dhamal.
  • Rajasthan: Kalbelia, Terah Tali and Kachchhi Ghodi.
  • Eastern India: 3 regional styles of Chhau.
  • North-eastern community pairs: Bodo-Bagurumba, Garo-Wangala and Reang-Hojagiri.
  • Dance-instrument pairs: Dollu Kunitha-dollu and Pung Cholom-pung, with Pung Cholom belonging to Manipur in north-eastern India.
  • Trap: A correct state association does not necessarily establish that a dance is exclusive to that state.

[References: Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 2, printed pp. 14-16; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, pp. 113-121; Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Lok Sabha Starred Question 107, 11 December 2023, Annexure II; SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, Folk Dances of India; Rajasthan Foundation, Dance Forms of Rajasthan; Eastern Zonal Cultural Centre, state cultural profiles; state government cultural and tourism portals of Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka, Telangana, Kerala, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Sikkim; UNESCO individual intangible cultural heritage element records.
